book.title: The Gevher Nesibe Hospital and Medical School

pages.title: A Hospital Ahead of Its Time
pages.content:
The Gevher Nesibe Complex in Kayseri is the oldest Anatolian Seljuk hospital still standing today. It is also the world’s first example of a hospital and a medical school built together in one place. In the 13th century, this place offered both theoretical education and practical training by the patients’ bedside. This systematic medical training did not appear in Europe until the 16th and 17th centuries. In fact, even the Imperial Medical School (Mekteb-i Tıbbiyye-i Adliyye-i Şâhâne), which was built by the Ottoman Sultan Mahmud II, opened more than 600 years after the Medical School in Kayseri.

When the Gevher Nesibe Hospital was opened, Konya was the capital of the Anatolian Seljuk State. At that time, Kayseri was also accepted as a second capital and was known as ‘Makarr-ı Ulemâ’ (the center of scientists).

This medical center was built by the Anatolian Seljuk ruler Gıyâseddin Keyhusrev I for his sister, Gevher Nesibe Sultan. Today, it serves as the Museum of the Seljuk Civilization (Selçuklu Uygarlığı Müzesi).

pages.title: A Princess and a Commander
pages.content: Gevher Nesibe Sultan was the daughter of Kılıçarslan II and the sister of Gıyâseddin Keyhusrev I. According to a famous story, she fell in love with a young commander when she was a young girl. However, her elder brother, Sultan Gıyâseddin Keyhusrev I, was against this relationship and did not allow them to marry. Instead, he wanted his sister to marry a palace official. Gevher Nesibe opposed this decision. To separate his sister from the commander, the Sultan sent the young man away to war. Some time later, the commander died in battle. Gevher Nesibe became very sad and fell ill with tuberculosis. Because there was no good hospital in Kayseri, she sadly died at a young age. On her deathbed, her brother apologized to her and asked for her final wish.

pages.title: The Last Wish
pages.content:
As the legend goes, Gevher Nesibe Sultan made a final request in her last days:

“I have a very serious illness, and there is no cure for it. No doctor has been able to heal me, and I am on my deathbed. Please use all my wealth to build a hospital to honor my memory. Let this hospital treat patients and look for cures for terrible diseases. Let famous doctors and surgeons be trained here. Nobody should pay any money. Let this place be a free charity in my name.”

pages.title: The Twin Madrasas
pages.content: To follow his sister’s wish, Gıyâseddin Keyhusrev built a madrasa (Gıyâsiye Medresesi) and a hospital (Şifâiye). The construction of the hospital lasted two years. Gevher Nesibe Sultan was buried in her tomb inside the madrasa. Because the two buildings are next to each other, people call them the ‘Twin Madrasas.’ According to the writing on the main gate of the hospital, it was built in 1205–1206.

pages.title: Learning Beside the Patients
pages.content: In the 13th century, medical education here was both theoretical and practical. Students learned theory at the Gıyâsiye and practiced at the Şifâiye. Historical studies show that the buildings had an underfloor heating system. It used steam from a bathhouse nearby. Students probably lived in small rooms inside the complex. In the summer, classes were held in the spacious courtyards. Doctors also examined daily outpatients in these areas. We do not know for sure, but historians think there was a chief doctor with assistants. The staff also had at least two general doctors, two surgeons, and a pharmacist. This staff was very similar to the one at the Keykâvus Hospital in Sivas.

pages.title: Great Teachers and Books
pages.content: Many famous scientists and doctors taught at this institution. Some of them were Sadreddin Konevî and Ekmeleddin al-Nahcuvânî, who was Mevlânâ’s close friend and doctor. Another important doctor was Kutbüddin eş-Şîrâzî, who was a famous eye doctor. At the Gıyâsiye, these scientists taught philosophy, religion, languages, and how the human body works. Students studied the most important medical books of the era, especially the works of er-Râzî and İbn Sînâ. They also read Arabic translations of ancient Greek and Roman doctors like Hippocrates and Galen. On the other hand, practical medical training took place at patients’ bedsides in the Şifâiye Hospital.

pages.title: Inside the Buildings
pages.content:
A corridor connects the madrasa and the hospital, and each one has a closed courtyard. Both buildings include a courtyard with a pool and rooms of different sizes. All the doors are small and open into covered walkways. None of the rooms have fireplaces or chimneys. There was no kitchen space inside the center. This shows that people brought meals from an outdoor kitchen.

The Gevher Nesibe Hospital had three operating rooms, and two surgeons worked there. Small windows at the top of these rooms provided dim light, which made it easier to control the light during operations. Doctors probably performed minor surgeries and cataract operations here.

pages.title: Medical Education at the Dârüşşifâ
pages.content:
The educational method of that era was based on the master-apprentice model. Students who graduated received an icâzet (diploma). This document listed the names of their teachers and older scientists in a line of tradition. Students who took classes at this madrasa were known as ‘dânişmend.’

Education at the hospital had two main parts. The first stage included classes in mathematics, astronomy, physics, languages, philosophy, and medicine. This stage was called ‘dârü’l-ilim’. In the second stage, students learned Islamic sciences. Treatment methods were based on the ideas of famous scientists like Bîrûnî and İbn Sînâ. Doctors prepared medicines using the best medical recipes of that time. Historical documents show that students also learned by observing doctors at patients’ bedsides. The hospital continued to provide medical care to patients until the early 20th century.

pages.title: Music Therapy at the Dârüşşifâ
pages.content: In his work Kitâbü’ş-Şifâ, İbn Sînâ (known as Avicenna in the West) stated that one of the best ways to treat patients is to make their minds and spirits stronger. He believed that giving them courage through their loved ones and using music can help them heal. Er-Râzî also noted that doctors should treat sad and stressed patients with music. At the same time, Fârâbî studied how different musical modes (makams) affect the human soul. He divided these modes into groups based on feelings, such as joy, fear, or comfort. He also explained which mode is best at specific times of the day. It is clear that experts used music therapy at the Gevher Nesibe Hospital.

pages.title: A Legacy That Lives On
pages.content:
Throughout history, there have been many examples of hospitals and medical schools. However, none of them combined both into a single building like the Gevher Nesibe Hospital. When we compare it to the first famous medical universities, such as Salerno, Bologna, and Paris, the Gevher Nesibe Hospital was more advanced in many ways. This hospital and madrasa came from centuries of collective knowledge. They show the great success of scholars in the Islamic world who lived during the 9th, 10th, and 11th centuries.

Gevher Nesibe Sultan never married the love of her life, but she won the hearts of many people and lived on even after her death.

exercises.title: Notice: Who Did It?
exercises.instructions: Sort the sentences: is the doer named, or not named?
exercises.question: When does the book name the doer?

items: This medical center was built by the Anatolian Seljuk ruler Gıyâseddin Keyhusrev I.
the Imperial Medical School, which was built by the Ottoman Sultan Mahmud II
Gevher Nesibe Sultan was buried in her tomb inside the madrasa.
In the summer, classes were held in the spacious courtyards.
Students who took classes at this madrasa were known as ‘dânişmend.’

The doer is named (by …): This medical center was built by the Anatolian Seljuk ruler Gıyâseddin Keyhusrev I.
the Imperial Medical School, which was built by the Ottoman Sultan Mahmud II
The doer is not named: Gevher Nesibe Sultan was buried in her tomb inside the madrasa.
In the summer, classes were held in the spacious courtyards.
Students who took classes at this madrasa were known as ‘dânişmend.’

exercises.explanation: The passive puts the result first. The book adds “by + doer” when the doer is important (a sultan). When the doer is clear or not important, it leaves it out.

feedback.correct: Good. Some passives name the doer; others do not.
feedback.incorrect: Look for the word by.

exercises.title: Notice: How Sure Is the Writer?

The hospital had three operating rooms.
The bathhouse has a dome on top.

feedback.incorrect: Look for a word that shows the writer is not sure.

exercises.explanation: “Instead” gives a different plan. “Because” gives a reason. “To + verb” at the start gives a purpose.

feedback.incorrect: Is each gap a different plan, a reason or a purpose?

Students learned by [choice] doctors at patients’ bedsides.

exercises.explanation: “Allow + person + to + verb”, “continue to + verb”, and “by + -ing” for a method.

feedback.correct: Correct. To marry, to provide, observing.
feedback.incorrect: Check the pattern after allow, continued and by.

transformItems.frame: Today, it is [blank] as the Museum of the Seljuk Civilization.

exercises.title: Use: A Place That Helps People

exercises.question: Who built it, what does it do, and why is it important?
exercises.explanation: Example: “The public library in my town was built in 1985. It serves as a place for reading, studying and meeting. It probably has more than 50,000 books. Students who have no quiet room at home study there. Nobody pays to use it. It is important because it helps everyone learn. Like the Gevher Nesibe Hospital, it is a gift to the community.”
